cues.text: From Governor to Friar
Born in 1386 at Capestrano in the Abruzzi region of the Kingdom of Naples, John trained in law at Perugia.
He became governor of that city in 1412, working against civic corruption before being captured during a local war in 1416.
During his captivity, a profound spiritual conversion led him to abandon his civil career entirely and enter the Franciscan Order.
Reformer and Papal Envoy
As a Friar Minor of the strict Observant reform, John became a close collaborator of St. Bernardine of Siena in promoting stricter Franciscan discipline.

Successive popes repeatedly entrusted him with sensitive diplomatic missions — opposing the antipope Felix V in Milan and Burgundy, negotiating with the King of France, and serving as papal nuncio to Austria, where he preached extensively against the Hussite heresy.
A Preaching Mission Against the Turks
After the catastrophic fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453, Pope Calixtus III commissioned the aging John, then nearly seventy, to preach a crusade for the defense of Christian Europe.
Finding little response in Bavaria and Austria, he concentrated his efforts in Hungary, directly threatened by the advancing Ottoman army under Sultan Mehmed II.
The Siege of Belgrade

In the summer of 1456, John personally raised and led a poorly equipped but highly motivated force of peasants and local landowners to reinforce the Hungarian commander John Hunyadi at the besieged fortress of Belgrade .
Holding aloft a crucifix and reportedly crying 'Victory, Jesus, victory!'
at the height of the fighting, John led his own contingent into battle.
That battle finally broke the Ottoman siege, a victory still commemorated by the Church's practice of ringing bells at noon, instituted in thanksgiving for the relief of Belgrade.
A Complicated Legacy
John's zeal as a reformer and preacher had a darker side historians have not ignored: as an inquisitor, he pursued the suppression of heresy with considerable severity.
In Poland, he actively pressed King Casimir IV to revoke protections previously granted to Jewish communities, contributing to persecutions in several Polish towns.
This record sits uneasily alongside his later celebrated role at Belgrade and reflects the harsher currents of his era's religious conflict.
Legacy

Worn out by the exertions of the campaign, John contracted plague from the unsanitary conditions common to armies of the era and died at Ilok, in modern Croatia, on October 23, 1456, just months after his victory.
Canonized in 1690, he is remembered as the 'Soldier Saint,' patron of military chaplains and jurists, and the namesake of the Franciscan mission at San Juan Capistrano in California.
